query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Engineering the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) via tailored thermomechanical processing and minor compositional tuning to produce a nanohierarchical microstructure will promote the in‐situ formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline oxide glaze layer during sliding. This occurs through the enhanced oxide precipitation enabled by the tailored microstructure, which acts as an adaptive lubricating film that maintains low friction and reduced wear across the full temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional, coarse‐grained CoCrFeNi HEA matrix without engineered microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Apply a processing route (or slight compositional adjustment) that induces a nanohierarchical, composition-undulated microstructure in the CoCrFeNi alloy. This modification is designed to encourage the formation of a strong and deformable oxide layer during sliding.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding in air over a temperature range from room temperature up to 800 °C, under typical normal loads and sliding speeds as employed in comparable tribological tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanohierarchical grain structure with controlled composition fluctuations that facilitate enhanced oxide precipitation and interfacial adhesion of the glaze layer.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, frictional heating and mechanical stress trigger the rapid formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline oxide layer on the wear surface. This in-situ formed glaze acts as a stable, self-lubricating film that minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact. At elevated temperatures, the designed microstructure ensures that the oxide film remains adherent and effective despite matrix softening, thereby reducing both friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi HEA, the processed alloy is expected to exhibit a lower and more stable coefficient of friction (with fewer fluctuations) and a significantly reduced wear rate (potentially achieving ultra-low values on the order of 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁶ mm³/N·m) across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Standard CoCrFeNi HEA without the nanohierarchical microstructure, which shows higher friction coefficient fluctuations and increased wear rate, especially at elevated temperatures due to insufficient oxide protection.
generation.boundary: Findings are expected under dry sliding conditions in ambient air, with contact parameters similar to those used in previous tribological experiments (e.g., loads between 5 and 30 N, sliding speeds around 0.2 m/s, and sliding distances comparable to 360 m). The lubrication mechanism relies on the natural formation of oxides; thus, environments that do not permit oxidation may not yield similar benefits.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the optimal processing parameters and minor alloying additions necessary to reliably induce the desired microstructure and oxide formation, as well as the robustness of the oxide film under cyclic and variable load conditions. Further work is needed to quantify the exact improvements in friction and wear performance across the full temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one processed via conventional methods (baseline) and one processed with the intervention to induce a nanohierarchical structure. Conduct controlled dry sliding wear tests in air at several temperatures (e.g., 25 °C, 400 °C, and 800 °C) using identical normal loads (e.g., 10 N) and sliding speeds (e.g., 0.2 m/s) over a fixed sliding distance. Monitor the friction coefficient in real time and perform post-test wear track profilometry and microstructural (e.g., SEM/EDS) analysis.
measurements: Real-time recording of friction coefficient curves.
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis to verify the presence and continuity of the oxide glaze layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention sample does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the average friction coefficient and the wear rate, along with clear evidence of a continuous, adherent oxide layer (compared to the baseline) across the entire temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

With the increase in load, the sliding parts were pressed against each other and it resulted in higher pressure at the interface. More resistance is offered by the counterparts during sliding owing to a higher pressure which results in higher friction at higher loads. Additionally, the soft matrix around the reinforcement easily wears out at higher loads which in turn results in contact between reinforcement protrusions and hard counterpart. This sliding of two harder phases results in a higher coefficient of friction. The CoF values increase considerably with an increase in sliding velocity as depicted in Fig. 7a–e. There is a chance of mechanically mixed layer formation at the sliding interface when parts are sliding at lower velocities. The presence of a mechanically mixed layer serves to prevent direct contact between sliding components, resulting in the lower CoF. In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals.
